findings.explanation: This custom role's permissions list covers compute.firewalls.*, compute.networks.*, and compute.subnetworks.* only — there is no compute.routers.* or compute.regionOperations.get permission, yet the module (google_compute_network.vpc.tf) creates google_compute_router.vpc and google_compute_router_nat.vpc. Git history confirms the drift: this file was last modified at commit a3df01d, while the router/NAT resources were added afterward in 048f2f7 ("replace default-gateway egress route with Cloud NAT"). A rules engine checks each resource's own attributes and can't cross-reference a hand-generated IAM permission list against a separate resource file to notice it fell out of sync. Anyone applying this module using only the terraform_pike role will get a permission-denied on the router/NAT resources, and the role no longer reflects the actual least-privilege footprint it claims to enforce.
findings.remediation: Regenerate .pike/pike.generated_policy.tf via the pike tool against the current module so it picks up google_compute_router and google_compute_router_nat. If pike isn't available, manually add compute.routers.create, compute.routers.get, compute.routers.update, compute.routers.delete, and compute.regionOperations.get (routers/NAT are regional resources, unlike the existing compute.globalOperations.get entry which only covers the global network/firewall resources).
findings.title: Generated least-privilege IAM role predates Cloud Router/NAT resources it should cover

findings.explanation: Every other value in this module is variable-driven (name, region, ip_cidr_range, secondary_ip_range — see variables.tf), but this firewall rule's protocol, port (tcp/8080), and source_tags ("web") are fully hardcoded with no corresponding variable. It also sets no target_tags or target_service_accounts, so HLD_GCP_074 (target_tags must match an instance tag) never fires — there's nothing to mismatch — but the practical effect is the rule applies to every instance in the VPC, not a scoped subset. The resource name "pike" and the 8080 test-style port line up with the pike-generated artifacts elsewhere in this repo (.pike/pike.generated_policy.tf, project pike-477416), suggesting this rule may exist to satisfy HLD_GCP_093 ("VPC networks must have at least one explicit firewall rule") or a pike validation exercise rather than representing an intentional security decision every consumer of this published module should inherit. Every environment that pulls this module gets an ingress allow for tcp/8080 from any "web"-tagged instance to every instance in the VPC, without opting in.
findings.remediation: Either remove this firewall rule from the base network module (application-specific ingress belongs in the consuming workload, not a general-purpose network module) or parameterize protocol/port/source_tags/target_tags via variables so consumers must explicitly opt in to what's allowed.
findings.title: Hardcoded, non-parameterized firewall rule bakes an app-specific port into a generic network module

findings.explanation: HLD_GCP_066 only checks that NAT log_config.enable is true, which it is — but the filter is set to "ERRORS_ONLY", so successful NAT translations are never logged. That's inconsistent with the rest of the module: the subnet's flow logs use aggregation_interval=INTERVAL_10_MIN, flow_sampling=0.5, and metadata=INCLUDE_ALL_METADATA (google_compute_subnetwork.sub.tf:14-18), and the firewall log_config also uses metadata=INCLUDE_ALL_METADATA (google_compute_firewall.tf:16-18). Every other surface is tuned for maximum visibility; NAT alone drops the connection records needed to trace which internal instance translated to which external IP/port — exactly the audit trail most useful during an incident.
findings.remediation: Change log_config.filter on google_compute_router_nat.vpc from "ERRORS_ONLY" to "ALL" to match the visibility level configured on the subnet flow logs and firewall logs.
findings.title: Cloud NAT logs only errors while every other logging surface in the module captures full metadata
